If the value from each piece remains equal, changes in cost influence the count only by the amount affordable. So, when price drops, they buy more proportionally, and when price rises, less. - selection sort always does O(n^2) comparisons and O(n) swaps. insertion sort on sorted array does O(n) comparisons and 0 swaps. so insertion sort is more efficient, not selection. so A is false.

B) the number of comparisons for selection sort depends on the initial arrangement of elements.
- selection sort always does fixed comparisons regardless of arrangement. i.e., (n-1)+(n-2)+...+1 comparisons. so B is false.

C) the number of data movements in selection sort depends on the initial arrangement of elements.
- selection sort does at most 1 swap per pass, so O(n) swaps. doesn't depend on arrangement. false.

D) the number of comparisons for bubble sort is independent of the initial arrangement of elements.
- bubble sort can be optimized with a flag to stop early if no swaps. So if array is already sorted, it can exit after 1 pass with n-1 comparisons. so comparisons depend on arrangement. if not optimized, bubble sort always does full passes. but typical bubble sort implementations include early termination. so D likely false because optimized bubble sort's comparisons depend on arrangement.

E) the number of data movements in bubble sort is independent of the initial arrangement of elements.
- bubble sort swaps adjacent elements when out of order. number of swaps depends on number of inversions. sorted array: 0 swaps. reversed: many swaps. so false.

F) the number of comparisons for insertion sort is independent of the initial arrangement of elements.
- insertion sort comparisons depend on arrangement. sorted: 0 swaps and O(n) comparisons. unsorted: more comparisons. false.

G) the number of comparisons for selection sort is independent of the initial arrangement of elements.
- yes, selection sort always does fixed number of comparisons: (n-1)+(n-2)+...+1. so G is true.

- descending array: insertion sort is worst-case O(n^2) swaps and comparisons. selection sort is also O(n^2) comparisons but only O(n) swaps. comparison counts: insertion sort has ~n^2/2 comparisons in worst case. selection sort is n(n-1)/2. similar. swaps: insertion sort is O(n^2), selection is O(n). so selection sort has fewer data movements. depends on efficiency criterion. question says data movement is swap or reassignment. f) "if a hypothesis test is conducted at the 1% level, there is a 99% chance of not rejecting the null hypothesis." no, this is not true. the alpha is the chance of rejecting when h0 is true. the probability of not rejecting depends on power and truth of h0.

g) "the power of a test concerns its ability to detect a null hypothesis." no, power is about rejecting h0 when false, not detecting null.

h) "if there is sufficient evidence to reject a null hypothesis at the 10% level, then there is sufficient evidence to reject it at the 5% level." no, opposite. p-value might be 0.07, rejected at 10% but not 5%.

i) "if a hypothesis test is conducted at the 1% level, there is a 1% chance of rejecting the null hypothesis." similar to d and f, the 1% is conditional on h0 being true.
